input: I'm a master's student with one GPU. Why do language models still make things up, and what's still hard about catching it?
verdict: Same question with the recruit step. 80 papers, 74 in full, 186 of 195 quotes kept (95%), 73 s. Worse: searches included the reader's hardware ("one GPU") and broad terms, so off-topic papers came in; the three two-group problems were boilerplate (a modest dataset, a fixed prompt, distribution shift across unrelated fields), and one title described a line the check had dropped. Fixed: recruit step removed, hardware kept out of searches, trimmed groups retitled from the checked claim, that boilerplate filtered. Not saved as an example.
search: Searching arXiv for “language model hallucination detection”, “one GPU”, “retrieval-augmented generation”, “faithfulness checking in LLMs”, “uncertainty estimation”, “language model hallucination”, “factuality evaluation”, “faithfulness checking”

terms.meaning: when a language model generates text that sounds plausible but contains false or made-up information
methods used to check whether statements generated by AI align with known facts or reliable sources
verifying that a model's output stays true to its input or given context, avoiding unsupported additions
techniques that help models express when they are unsure, reducing confident but incorrect answers
a method where models look up external information before answering to improve accuracy and reduce fabrication

sentences.text: Language models still hallucinate because they mimic linguistic patterns instead of performing axiomatic reasoning, and their errors span factual, cultural, linguistic, and logical dimensions [2607.08403, 2605.17007].

Catching hallucinations is hard because automated factuality judges are systematically biased against human judgments, with misalignment driven by structured failure modes like incomplete evidence and unverifiable claims rather than just low confidence [2609.00494].

The core evaluation trade-off, atomic facts lose essential context while broader statements lose granularity, makes precise verification difficult, and uncertainty itself stems from multiple interacting sources that are hard to disentangle [2608.05228, 2606.32012].

Current detection methods often require full autoregressive generations, but recent work shows partial-generation or even input-only uncertainty estimation can be effective, suggesting we can catch problems earlier and cheaper [2605.06053].

read_first.why: Explains why automated judges fail and how human-anchored evaluation works
Shows the granularity-context trade-off that makes verification fundamentally hard
Demonstrates a multi-agent approach that reduces hallucinations by 79%
Presents low-cost uncertainty estimation usable on one GPU
Benchmarks hallucination across reasoning, cultural, and linguistic dimensions

problems.title: Limited coverage of rare domains and edge cases due to moderate dataset size

statements.quote: First, although the dataset is carefully curated to include hallucination-prone questions, its size remains moderate compared to large-scale QA benchmarks, potentially limiting coverage of rare domains and edge cases.
statements.label: limited coverage of rare domains and edge cases due to moderate dataset size

statements.quote: the MMLongBench benchmark focuses predominantly on government reports, and the system’s performance on other scientific domains (e.g., biomedical, legal) remains unvalidated.
statements.label: performance unvalidated in other scientific domains

problems.explanation: The HalluScore benchmark stays moderate in size, so rare topics and edge cases in Arabic hallucination detection get little coverage. The multimodal RAG paper shows a similar gap: its MMLongBench benchmark centers on government reports and has not been tested on biomedical or legal texts. Wider domain coverage would let researchers see whether hallucination patterns hold across very different knowledge areas.
problems.first_step: Clone the repository from "Multimodal Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Scientific Document Understanding using Open-Source SLMs" at https://github.com/AlexandruSauca/Multimodal-Advanced-RAG-using-local-SLMs-for-PDF-document-understanding and run its retrieval pipeline on a small public set of biomedical PDFs such as PubMed Central open-access articles to see how chunk retrieval and answer quality change compared with the reported government-report results.

problems.title: Sensitivity to prompt formulation and decoding strategies not evaluated

statements.quote: Finally, the evaluation relies on a fixed prompting setup, and model performance may vary under different prompt formulations or decoding strategies.
statements.label: sensitivity to prompt formulation and decoding strategies not evaluated

statements.quote: Although beam decoding is adopted by most publicly available AMR parsers and therefore provides a consistent evaluation setting across models, the behaviour of uncertainty under alternative decoding strategies (e.g., sampling-based or diverse decoding methods) remains unexplored and may yield different candidate distributions and reliability characteristics.
statements.label: uncertainty behavior under non-beam decoding strategies

problems.explanation: Both benchmarks evaluate with a single prompt template and beam decoding, so it is unknown how much scores swing when the prompt wording changes or when sampling-based decoding replaces beam search. The AMR parser paper notes that beam search gives a consistent setting but leaves the behavior under diverse decoding entirely unexplored. Mapping that sensitivity would tell practitioners whether a single reported number is trustworthy.
problems.first_step: Use the code from "How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing" at https://github.com/naist-nlp/UE_Method_AMR_Parser to run the same parser on its validation set with three decoding modes, beam search, top-k sampling, and nucleus sampling, and record the Prediction Rejection Ratio for each mode.

problems.title: Policy degradation under distribution shift

statements.quote: FSA-guided ASI relies on residual structure learned from historical or calibration data. Its efficiency depends on this structure remaining stable across the evaluation population, i.e., model updates, retrieval or grounding changes, shifts in user queries, or new failure modes can degrade the policy.
statements.label: policy degradation under distribution shift

statements.quote: Under concept drift (A1 violated), STAMP degrades predictably.
statements.label: Method fails when assumption A1 (concept stability) is violated

problems.explanation: FSA-guided ASI leans on a residual structure learned from past data; when the model, retriever, or user queries shift, that structure can stale and the policy degrades. STAMP shows a parallel effect: under concept drift its source-only predictor loses accuracy in a predictable way. Understanding the degradation curve helps decide when to re-calibrate or re-train.
problems.first_step: Recreate the STAMP correlation-ratio η² calculation from the paper "STAMP: Predicting Out-of-Distribution Generalization without Target Data" using a public image classification backbone (e.g., ResNet-50) trained on ImageNet, then evaluate η² on a sequence of increasingly shifted test sets such as ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and ImageNet-A to plot the degradation trend.

problems.title: Bias toward Arabic cultural knowledge limits generalizability to broader domains

statements.quote: its adaptation to entirely new domains or tasks still relies heavily on an offline construction and optimization process.
statements.label: requires offline rebuild for new domains

statements.quote: when a new domain introduces unfamiliar concepts, terminologies, or relational structures, the system typically requires offline rebuilding, retraining, or re-indexing before it can achieve strong performance, rather than adapting immediately during deployment.
statements.label: no immediate adaptation to novel domains

problems.explanation: The FD-RAG framework requires an offline rebuild whenever a new domain brings unfamiliar terms or relational structures, so it cannot adapt on the fly during deployment. That rigidity makes it costly to extend beyond the original knowledge silos. A system that could ingest new schemas incrementally would cut the re-indexing cycle dramatically.
problems.first_step: Implement a minimal dual-system RAG loop inspired by "FD-RAG: Federated Dual-System Retrieval-Augmented Generation" using a lightweight local encoder (e.g., sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2) for the memory side and a small open LLM for the generation side, then measure how many new legal-clause PDFs can be added to the memory index before generation quality drops below a threshold.

problems.title: Chunk size selection lacks systematic evaluation

statements.quote: Despite its importance, chunk size is often selected without proper evaluation of its impact on generation quality.
statements.label: chunk size selection lacks systematic evaluation

problems.explanation: Chunk size directly shapes retrieval precision, context completeness, and compute cost, yet practitioners usually pick a size by habit rather than evidence. The dedicated paper argues that no systematic evaluation exists across generation quality metrics. A controlled sweep would give the first principled guidance.
problems.first_step: Follow the experimental design outlined in "The Effect of Text Chunk Size on Retrieval-Augmented Generation Performance" by building a tiny RAG pipeline (dense retriever + small generator) and running a grid search over chunk sizes (128, 256, 512, 1024 tokens) on the public HotpotQA development set, logging retrieval recall, answer F1, and latency for each setting.

problems.title: Activation pair choice affects accuracy-calibration balance

statements.quote: A limitation is that the activation pair influences the trade-off between predictive performance and calibration
statements.label: activation pair choice affects accuracy-calibration balance

problems.explanation: Stochastic nonlinearities let each unit randomly pick between activation functions during a forward pass, but the paper notes that the specific pair of activations chosen shifts the balance between predictive accuracy and calibration quality. Knowing which pairs favor which side would let designers match the nonlinearity to the downstream risk profile.
problems.first_step: Reproduce the core experiment from "Stochastic Nonlinearities Improve Uncertainty Estimation" by training a small CNN on CIFAR-100 with three different activation pairs (ReLU+GELU, Swish+Mish, ReLU+SiLU) under the same stochastic switching schedule, then compare test accuracy and expected calibration error.
